label: Rappaport explicitly models ritual as both transducer and homeostat.
The pig herd does not trigger kaiko by exceeding ecological carrying capacity.
The “algorithmic on/off switch” is not source-attested machinery.
The apparent ecological trigger passes through women’s labor and decision pressure.
The ritual cycle regulates when warfare can resume.
Rappaport adds ecological effects to ritual rather than proving symbolism irrelevant.
Rappaport quantifies the ecological system but does not supply a mathematical cybernetic model.
Sahlins attacks ecological functional explanation at the level of what counts as utility.
Chomsky supplies an analogy for generativity, not the genealogy of habitus.
Habitus generates regularity precisely without functioning as a rule book.
Habitus is generative, but its possibility space is historically bounded.
Practical competence generates moves that no explicit rule can pre-enumerate.
“Algorithm” is actually Bourdieu’s word—but only in a specific analogy.
Habitus generates both practices and the classifications through which practices become meaningful.
Habitus is incorporated into posture and practice, not stored as a purely cognitive rule set.
Piaget appears inside Bourdieu’s account of practical schemes, but the claimed genealogy remains unproven.
Habitus is meant to dissolve the agency/determinism opposition, not mediate between two intact poles.
Culture is a degree of population distribution, not a superorganic substance.
Culture is not confined to representations inside individual minds.
Cultural transmission is transformation with replication as the limiting case.
“Cognitive virus” overstates the epidemiological analogy Sperber himself restricts.
A cultural attractor is a statistical pattern, not a force pulling representations.
Cultural attraction is not dictated by evolved cognitive biases alone.
Sperber’s source formalism is a simple transformation matrix, not a developed dynamical phase-space model.
Later cultural epidemiology explicitly includes practices, artifacts, and institutions.
Calling a cultural form “contagious” names the distribution to explain; it does not explain its persistence.
Institutional structure is not absent from Sperber’s later naturalistic architecture.
Autopoiesis originally names recursive component production, not generic self-maintenance.
Luhmann explicitly refuses a literal transfer of biological autopoiesis into sociology.
Luhmann replaces persons and actions with communication as the elementary operation of social systems.
Operational closure means autonomous operation under environmental dependence, not social isolation.
Luhmann explicitly rejects the simple input-transform-output machine as a model of law.
A specific Varela-to-Luhmann technical transfer can actually be documented.
“Environment” is a system-relative location, not Luhmann’s synonym for irrelevance.
Luhmann removes action from the substrate of society but does not remove action from the theory.
Functional differentiation is not institutional statecraft directed from a center.
“X counts as Y in C” is a constitutive-rule schema, not a computational algorithm.
Constitutive rules can recursively build institutional levels on top of prior statuses.
Declarations are Searle’s speech-act category, not an imported formal-logic operator.
Collective intentionality alone does not generate institutional reality.
The operative consequence of institutional status is deontic power.
Institutional reality is ontologically dependent yet epistemically objective.
Money is not exhausted by the physical token that bears monetary status.
Institutional status can emerge before an explicit constitutive rule exists.
Language is constitutive of institutional status, but Searle does not identify representation with computation.
Searle offers a conceptual ontology, not an empirical proof that all society executes one mechanism.
Interdisciplinary “import” has at least four different depths that the graph currently conflates.
Three branches independently produce cultural order without explicit rule execution.
The deepest formal move in the graph is choosing what kinds of things are allowed to exist.
Across otherwise incompatible theories, the same present input need not produce the same cultural consequence.
“X counts as Y” leaves open the prior problem of who can successfully make it count.
Formalization repeatedly gains operational clarity by manufacturing a remainder it can no longer express.
Programming languages do not require deterministic state transitions.
Computational state is one semantic representation, not a necessary primitive of programming languages.
“Prompt language” is not yet a single technically stable language category.
Markup and computation are orthogonal properties, not mutually exclusive categories.
Markdown is a plain-text formatting syntax, not formally a “subset of markup.”
“Domain-specific” describes scope, not computational status.
Modeling language and executable language are not mutually exclusive.
A specification language can define executable state transitions without becoming implementation code.
Pseudocode stops being pseudocode when its ambiguity is replaced by specified machine-checkable semantics.
A generative grammar formally determines a language of strings; it does not by itself specify artifact semantics.
The proposed language taxonomy collapses several independent axes into mutually exclusive labels.
Genuine conversation is not fully precomputable by either participant.
ActionWorkflow’s formal loop explicitly depends on an informal shared background.
ActionWorkflow crosses from conversational theory into an executable workflow language and runtime.
The Coordinator literally compiled conversational roles into finite-state permitted-move tables.
The Coordinator repaired network message order before applying conversational state transitions.
Intent is interactionally accomplished rather than simply encoded before an utterance.
Suchman’s political target is the conversion of analytic categories into compulsory organizational actions.
DEMO separates organizational semantics from their informational and technical realization.
DEMO turns organizational action into explicit state-transition semantics.
DEMO’s formal communicative acts still require culture to determine their relational effect.
Conditions of satisfaction have an uncompiled cultural dependency.
The menu is the executable surface of the conversational ontology.
The Coordinator turns an unfinished social obligation into a persistent data object.
The Coordinator localizes the names of moves while preserving their underlying formal structure.
The Coordinator manufactures a total conversational chronology from a distributed event stream.
The Coordinator can preserve ambiguity only by making ambiguity itself a formal conversational type.
The central dispute is not whether formalization loses reality, but what a knowingly incomplete formalization is allowed to do.
A performative inherits its force from a conventional procedure and its circumstances.
Authority enters speech-act theory as a condition on who may make an utterance count.
A promise is consequential because it reorganizes what later conduct counts as in order.
Explicit performatives clarify force without making context disappear.
The language/action perspective was built through hermeneutics, not speech-act theory alone.
Listening is interpretation against a shared but never fully explicit background.
Speech-act theory is explicitly a starting point that Winograd and Flores transform rather than simply implement.
The operative meaning of organizational language is relocated into commitments among participants.
Conversation for action specifies a normative possibility space, not merely a four-step script.
Conditions of satisfaction are constitutive yet disputable, not objective facts waiting to be checked.
The action that satisfies a request is not itself reducible to the conversation that coordinates it.
Winograd and Flores explicitly reject the goal of a complete background-free language for human understanding.
Agent-oriented programming makes a formally represented mental state part of program state.
AOP turns speech-act labels into typed communication primitives.
Shoham treats agent mental categories as useful approximations, not a uniquely correct ontology.
Executable mentalistic communication depends on behavioral assumptions linking internal attitudes to action.
Speech-act semantics for agents is rebuilt from joint intentions and teamwork.
Finite conversational structures can be treated as consequences of act semantics rather than primitive protocols.
Mentalistic ACL semantics relies on assumptions about agents communicating in good faith.
FIPA standardizes communicative acts as a shared machine-readable catalogue.
FIPA gives communicative acts formal preconditions and intended effects, turning felicity-like conditions into logic.
FIPA locates communicative-act semantics in beliefs, intentions, uncertainty, and rational effects.
Refusal becomes a formally typed communicative operation with specified semantic structure.
FIPA interaction protocols are explicitly pre-enumerated inter-agent plans.
A normative communication standard needs semantics whose compliance can be tested from a public perspective.
Conventional meaning can bind publicly even when private intention diverges.
Public communication semantics still depends on social context rather than message syntax alone.
Private intention is unsuitable as the normative ground of interoperability because autonomous agents cannot read one another’s minds.
Sequence-oriented protocols overconstrain autonomous agents by prescribing trajectories instead of interaction meaning.
A protocol action gets its public meaning from the social commitment it creates or changes.
Commitment protocols give social obligations explicit state-change operations in event calculus.
Commitment semantics lets agents plan alternative runtime paths while preserving social obligations.
